newsitem.title: USA: Pratt, GE hopeful on engine project.
newsitem.headline: Pratt, GE hopeful on engine project.

text.p: General Electric Co. and Pratt & Whitney said Tuesday they will work to keep their aircraft engine joint venture going despite Boeing Co.'s cancellation of its "superjumbo" jet.
"Nothing has cancelled the joint venture at this point," Pratt spokesman Mark Sullivan told Reuters. "The only question is the pace of development."
Boeing said late on Monday that it would halt development of its new, larger version of its 747 jumbo jet because of a lack of orders.
But a spokesman for GE Aircraft Engines stopped short of saying the partnership, formed last year to serve Boeing's planned longer-range 747, would definitely proceed.
"There's a desire to keep it going, but that's up to the market," GE Aircraft Engines spokesman Rick Kennedy told Reuters.

The move left Airbus Industrie alone in the market with a proposed all-new superjumbo plane that could seat 600 passengers, compared with 416 in a typical three-class configuration for the current-generation 747-400.
Kennedy said there was no point proceeding with such a costly project unless there was some assurance there was a market for the new engine.
"We've got to sit down with Pratt and decide what direction we want to go in, and then we've got to sit down with Boeing and Airbus," said Kennedy.
Pratt & Whitney is a unit of United Technologies Corp.
Traditional rivals Pratt and GE had planned to spend a combined $750 million to get their joint engine ready by the end of the year 2000, officials of both companies have said.
"We will continue to have discussions with Boeing and Airbus" about the so-called GP 7000 engine, said Sullivan.
"Boeing's needs are obviously not as urgent as they had been, but we just don't know until we understand their full production plans for the 767, 777 and 747," said Sullivan.
GE and Pratt had planned to develop a different model of the same engine for a European Airbus jet.
"Both companies are extremely pleased with how the joint venture has worked to date," said Sullivan. "Both from a business and technical perspective, we really like the way the engine is looking."
"We like the way the two businesses are working together, so now we have to find where our customers are going to take us."
"We'd like to find a way to keep it going," said Sullivan.
